entries.title: The Shepherd Who Looks After Me
entries.text:
Yahweh is the shepherd who looks after me.
I will never lack anything.
entries.reflection:
A shepherd stays close to the sheep. He watches the path, the weather, and where the grass and water are. The sheep don't have to figure all of that out alone. Psalm 23 begins with that picture. Yahweh is the shepherd who looks after me.

The next line says, "I will never lack anything." The rest of the psalm shows what that care looks like. "He makes me lie down in meadows of fresh grass." "He restores my strength." He guides down right roads because that is who he is. The promise is not that the path stays easy. Later the singer walks through a dark valley and says, "I am not afraid of harm, since you are with me." Wants and needs aren't always the same thing. Some days still feel short, short on time, or money, or peace. Those days are real. This psalm sets them inside a larger care. You are looked after, even in the valley, by a shepherd who walks the road with you.

So today you can ask for what you need. You can also notice what has already been given, even if it's only a meal and a place to sit down. Think of walking a familiar street after a long shift, turning the same worry over in your mind: will there be enough? The psalm would have you look beside you, not only at the lack. The shepherd is already on this road with you. You can walk it as someone who is known and kept, and you can lie down when he gives you rest. The psalm even speaks of a feast set in a hard place, and of goodness and faithful love that chase after the singer all his days. That is a different picture from barely getting by. Ask him to restore your strength, and to stay with you if the road turns dark before the day is over.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, my shepherd, look after me today. You see what I need, even the things I haven't said out loud. Thank you that you make your people lie down in safe places, and that you restore strength when it has run out. Lead me and keep me close. I have been walking a familiar road with a worried mind, wondering if there will be enough. Teach me to notice what you have already given, a meal, a place to sit, the fact that I am not alone on this path. When the way gets dark, stay with me so I do not have to be afraid of harm. Give me a quiet heart that can rest in your care, and thank you for walking this road with me. Guide me down the right roads, because that is who you are. Amen.

entries.title: A Hiding Place and Strength
entries.text:
God is our hiding place and our strength,
always ready to help in trouble.
entries.reflection:
Trouble isn't a surprise in this verse. It's part of the road, and God meets us there. He is our hiding place and our strength, always ready to help.

The psalm does not pretend the trouble is small. The next lines say, "So we will not be afraid when the earth shakes," or when mountains slide into the heart of the sea. That is a picture of a world coming apart, and still the people of God refuse to make fear their first word. Later they say, "Yahweh of Armies is on our side." A hiding place is where you can catch your breath and admit you're afraid. Strength is what helps you stand up again and take the next step. God is both at once. Always ready means his help doesn't make you wait until you've calmed down. You can turn to him while your hands are still shaking.

Picture yourself sitting in the car before a hard appointment, the engine off, not quite ready to open the door. That is a good place to pray this verse. Hiding here isn't disappearing from the people who need you. It's how you find your feet again. Rest long enough to stand, then go back to the work and the people in front of you. When a hard day comes, you can start with a simple prayer: be my shelter, and be my strength. He is already ready to help, even if the ground under the day feels unsteady. The psalm also speaks of a river that makes the city of God glad, and of help that comes when morning comes. You may not feel that gladness yet, sitting in the car with the engine off. You can still go to him as a hiding place first, and then as strength for the door you have to open.
entries.prayer: God, you are my hiding place and my strength. I'm bringing you the trouble I'm carrying, and I do not have to make it smaller than it is. Thank you that you are always ready to help, and that we do not have to wait until we feel brave. Shelter me. Give me strength for what's in front of me. I think of the moments when my hands shake, and of the car door I am not ready to open. Meet me there. Let me hide in you long enough to stand, then send me back to the people who need me. When the day feels like the ground is moving, remind me that you are on our side. I trust you with this trouble, and I thank you that I do not have to face it alone. Amen.

entries.title: Where You Put Your Weight
entries.text:
Trust Yahweh completely.
Do not lean on what you understand yourself.
entries.reflection:
"Trust Yahweh completely." Then the proverb tells you where not to put all your weight. Your own understanding is too small to carry everything.

The next line shows what trust looks like in practice: "Include him in everything you do," and then, "and he will make your paths straight." Right after that comes a warning that fits our verse well: "Do not think you are wise by yourself." This book also spends line after line teaching people to pay attention, to learn, and to choose with care. A mind that thinks is a gift. Trust and careful thought belong together. The warning is about leaning. When you lean, you rest your full weight on something. If the only thing holding you up is your own view of a situation, that view will sometimes be too thin. You can't see the end of a choice from the middle of it. You can't see what a year will ask of you.

To trust Yahweh is to include him in the choice, and to let his wisdom carry what yours cannot. Think of a decision you keep flipping over, a job, a bill, a conversation, as if turning it again will finally make the end of the path appear. Pray before you decide, even if the prayer is short and said at a red light. Ask for a clear mind and a humble one. Then act, with open hands, even while some questions are still unanswered. Including him is not a last stamp you add after you've already chosen. It's how you begin. The proverb does not tell you to stop thinking. It tells you not to rest your whole weight on what you can see from here. Bring him the choice, wait long enough to be honest, and then walk the path he makes straight, even if you only see the next piece of it.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, I trust you with this whole day. Give me a clear mind and a humble one. I have been leaning hard on my own understanding, turning the same choice over and over, hoping the end of the path will show itself. Forgive me for thinking I can be wise by myself. Include yourself in everything I do, and make my paths straight. Guide the decision in front of me, whether it is a job, a bill, or a conversation I have been delaying. Teach me to pray before I choose, even if the prayer is short. I place what I cannot see into your hands. Help me act with an open hand, and to come back to you if I start leaning on myself again. Amen.

entries.title: Brave While You Wait
entries.text:
Wait for Yahweh.
Be strong and brave in your heart.
Yes, wait for Yahweh.
entries.reflection:
"Wait for Yahweh." The psalm says it twice, with a charge in the middle: be strong and brave in your heart. Waiting and bravery are set side by side. This kind of waiting isn't doing nothing on the couch. It's a steady heart turned toward God while an answer is still on the way.

David has been asking God not to hide his face. He has already said, "Even if my own father and mother walk away," still "Yahweh will take me in." Just before our verse he makes a hard, hopeful claim: "I am sure I will see Yahweh’s goodness" while he is still alive on the earth. Then he tells his own heart to wait, and to be brave in the waiting. Most of us would rather hold the answer than hold the wait. We fill the quiet with worry, or we shove on a door because the right one hasn't opened yet. The strength this psalm names sits in the place where fear talks the loudest. Bravery there can look quiet from the outside. It can look like telling God the truth, keeping a promise you already made, or staying soft on a day when the way through is still hidden.

Yes, wait for Yahweh. He is worth waiting for. The thing you placed in his hands is still in his hands. If you are waiting for a phone call, or for a door that has not opened, you can do more than stare at the screen. You can be strong in your heart, and you can say again that you expect to see his goodness. Waiting like that can include a walk, a kept promise, or a meal you still have to make for someone else. The wait is real, and so is the bravery the psalm asks of your heart. God has not set the hope down.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, I'm waiting for you, and the wait is hard. Make my heart strong and brave while I wait. Keep me steady and honest. Thank you that you take your people in, even when other help walks away. Thank you that David could say he was sure he would see your goodness while he still lived on the earth. I want that kind of hope. I place this hope in your hands again, the phone call, the door that has not opened, the answer I do not have yet. Help me wait for you without filling the quiet with panic, and without shoving at a door you have not opened. Teach me to tell you the truth and to stay soft. I will wait for you. Amen.

entries.title: The God Who Does Not Get Tired
entries.text:
Do you not know? Have you not heard?
Yahweh is the everlasting God,
the Creator of the ends of the earth.
He does not get tired or worn out.
No one can measure his understanding.
entries.reflection:
Isaiah asks a question that works like a hand on your shoulder: Do you not know? Have you not heard? It's easy to forget the answer on a day when you're worn out. Yahweh is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not get tired or worn out. No one can measure his understanding.

The verse answers a complaint. Just before it, the people have been saying, "Yahweh does not see my way," and "and my God ignores my rights." Isaiah doesn't shame the tiredness. He reminds them who God is, and then he says what God does: "He gives strength to the tired." A little later comes the promise many of us know: "But those who wait for Yahweh will have their strength renewed." Set that next to a long evening, when the dishes are still in the sink and your mind is done. We run out of strength. Even the young stumble, the chapter says. He does not. Everlasting means he has no beginning and no end. Creator of the ends of the earth means the far places you'll never see are his, and so is the room where you're sitting.

That's a gift when your own thoughts have run out of road. You can bring him a problem you can't sort out. You can also bring him nothing but your tiredness. He is still listening, and he is not worn out. Wait for him. Ask him to give strength to the tired, and to renew what has run out, for today and not only for some later year. The chapter will not let us treat weariness as proof that God has gone missing. Young people stumble, it says, and still the everlasting God gives power to those who have none. You can sit in a tired room and tell him the truth, then wait for the strength he has promised to give.
entries.prayer: Everlasting God, you made the ends of the earth, and you never grow tired. I'm worn out, and I have questions I can't measure. Stay with me. I have sometimes felt as if you did not see my way, and I thank you that this chapter answers that feeling with who you are. You give strength to the tired. You renew the strength of those who wait for you. I bring you this long evening, the dishes, the finished mind, the problem I cannot sort out. Give me the strength I need for today. Teach me to wait for you instead of deciding that you have ignored me. I trust your understanding, which I cannot measure, and I ask you to lift my tired heart. Amen.

entries.title: Faithful and Present
entries.text: Nobody will withstand you as long as you live. I stood by Moses, and I will stand by you in the same way. You will find me faithful and present; I will not leave you.
entries.reflection:
These words were spoken to Joshua as he took up the work Moses had carried. God says he stood by Moses, and he will stand by Joshua in the same way. "You will find me faithful and present; I will not leave you."

Moses has died, and Joshua must now rise and lead the people across the Jordan into the land God promised. That is a heavy task, the kind that can keep you up at night. God doesn't first hand him a longer list. He speaks to that weight with a promise about his own character. He is faithful. He is present. He stays with the person he sends, and he doesn't walk off once the work gets hard. Right after our verse he says, "So be strong and brave." And near the end of the same speech: "Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go." Strength here is not a personality type. It grows out of a promise that God will be there.

Our days aren't Joshua's days, and our work is our own. What we can hold from this verse is the way God stays. When something in front of you feels too big, you can ask for that same company. Maybe you have been given a responsibility someone else used to carry, and the chair they left still feels too large. Tell him you need him to be faithful and present right here, in this room, with this task. Then take the step that's in front of you, with him beside you. Joshua still had to pack, speak to the people, and walk toward the river. The promise did not replace the work. It made bravery possible inside the work. If you have a Jordan of your own to cross, you can rise and do the next true thing because he has said he will not leave you.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, you are faithful and present. You stood with Moses, and you stood with Joshua, and you stay with your people still. This in front of me feels too big. Be with me in it. Thank you that you do not leave, and that you are with us wherever we go. I need that promise in this room, with this task, especially where I am taking up work someone else used to carry. Make me strong and brave, not because I feel ready, but because you are here. Help me take the next step with you beside me. When I am tempted to lose heart, remind me of your own words. I trust you to be faithful in what I cannot finish alone. Stay with me today. Amen.

entries.title: Close to the Brokenhearted
entries.text:
Yahweh is close to people with broken hearts.
He rescues those whose spirits are crushed.
entries.reflection:
Some pain makes a person feel far from everyone, and far from God as well. Psalm 34 says Yahweh is close to people with broken hearts. He rescues those whose spirits are crushed.

The heading of this psalm remembers a fearful day in David's life, when he pretended to be out of his mind in front of a king and then got away. It is not a poem written from a safe chair. Just before our verse it says that when good people cry out, Yahweh hears, and "He rescues them from every trouble." Just after it comes an honest line: "A good person may have many troubles," and then, "but Yahweh rescues him from every one." Close means near. God comes close to the person who is hurting. In this verse, a broken heart is a place he moves toward, not a place he avoids. Crushed is an honest word too. The psalm lets the hurt stay as large as it is. God comes anyway, and rescue is his real help.

Some losses are still losses this afternoon, and the ache may still be there when you sit on the edge of the bed at night. His rescue means you are met inside that hurt by someone who can actually help. You can tell him the true size of it, without cleaning it up first. Sit with this verse if your spirit feels crushed: he is close, and he rescues. You do not have to get yourself together before you cry out. David wrote these words after a day of fear, not after a day when everything had already been mended. Many troubles can still be true in the same life, and the psalm does not deny that. It says Yahweh hears, comes close, and rescues. Let that be the first thing you remember when the room is quiet and the hurt is not.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, you are close to people with broken hearts. Please come near to me. You know the true size of this hurt, and I do not want to clean it up before I speak. Thank you that you hear when your people cry out, and that you rescue them from trouble. A person may have many troubles, and I feel the weight of mine tonight. Stay close so I can tell you're here. Rescue me, and rescue those I love who also feel crushed. Meet me on the edge of the bed, and in the hours when the ache is still there. I trust you to come toward a broken heart, not to turn away from it. Hold me while I wait for your help, and let me rest in the fact that you are near. Amen.

entries.title: You Only Need to Keep Still
entries.text: Yahweh will fight for you. You only need to keep still.”
entries.reflection:
Some troubles get worse because you cannot stop poking at them. You lie awake and refresh a page. You rehearse tomorrow's conversation until the words are worn thin. The room is dark, and your mind is still at work, as if thinking hard enough could force a door open. Israel stood in a place like that, with the sea in front of them and an army behind, and Moses said, "Yahweh will fight for you. You only need to keep still."

They had just accused Moses of bringing them out to die. He told them, "Have no fear. Stay where you are, and you will see Yahweh rescue you today." The stillness he asks for has nothing lazy about it. He is telling them to stop frantic motion long enough to let God do what they cannot. A few breaths later Yahweh tells Moses, "Tell the Israelites to move forward." The sea will divide, and they will walk a path they could not have dug with their own hands. Stillness, then, does not close the story. It is the needed word in the hour when fear keeps grabbing the wheel. There is a time to wait, and there is a time to walk, and both belong to him.

Tonight, set the phone down. Leave the conversation unrehearsed for a little while. Tell Yahweh the thing you cannot fix, and keep still long enough to remember that he fights for his people. In the morning you may need to walk forward, as Israel did. You do not have to win the night by turning the same worry over and over. The fight that matters most is his, and you can rest in that before you sleep. If the fear comes back at two in the morning, say the verse again, and keep still a little longer, until sleep comes.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, I am tired of fighting in the dark. I keep refreshing the page, and I keep rehearsing words as if that could save me. Thank you that you fight for your people, and that I am allowed to keep still. I hand you the trouble I cannot fix. Help me put the phone down tonight, and help me stop turning the same worry over until morning. When it is time to move forward, give me the courage Israel needed at the sea. Until then, quiet my frantic motion. Rescue me in the way I cannot arrange for myself, and let me sleep as someone you are already defending. Amen.

entries.title: Hand Over Your Future
entries.text:
Hand over your future to Yahweh.
Trust him, and he will take action.
entries.reflection:
A future can sit in your mind like a weight you never put down. You turn it over at the bus stop, on the walk home, in the minutes before sleep: the job, the rent, the hope you are almost afraid to name. The worry can look like planning, and sometimes it is only fear dressed up as responsibility. The psalm gives you something better to do with that weight. "Hand over your future to Yahweh. Trust him, and he will take action."

The song has already said, "Find your joy in Yahweh, and he will give you what your heart asks." Then comes our verse, and after it a promise that "He will make your goodness shine like the dawn," along with "your fair treatment like the noonday sun." The psalm is not handing you a charm for getting every wish. It teaches a way of living in a land where other people seem to get ahead by doing wrong, and where waiting can feel like losing. A later line says, "Be still in front of Yahweh and wait calmly for him." Handing over your future does not mean you stop working or praying. It means the outcome is his to take action on, and you are not required to wrestle it all night.

When the bus is late and the day's plan starts to slip, practice the handing over in a small way. Say the future you are gripping, out loud if you can, and give it to him. Trust him to take action in the hours you cannot see yet. Then do the next honest thing in front of you, as someone whose hope is not fastened only to a schedule. The job still needs your work, and the rent still needs your care. You can do those things with open hands, instead of with a future clenched tight in your fist.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, I have been carrying my future as if it were a weight I was not allowed to set down. I turn it over at the bus stop and again before I sleep. Today I hand it to you. Thank you that you take action, and that I can trust you with what I cannot see yet. Teach me to find my joy in you, and to wait calmly when other people seem to get ahead. I do not want to wrestle this all night. Receive the job, the rent, and the hope I am almost afraid to name. Direct my next honest step, and hold the rest. I trust you. Amen.

entries.title: Better Together Than Alone
entries.text:
Two people are better off than one,
because they get more for their work together.
entries.reflection:
You can get used to doing everything by yourself. You carry the bags up the stairs in one trip because it seems easier than asking. You start a hard task on a quiet afternoon and never think to call anyone. After a while, the solitude can start to feel like strength, even when it is only habit, or pride, or the fear of being a bother. The Teacher looks at that kind of life and is not impressed. "Two people are better off than one, because they get more for their work together."

He has just described a person who is completely alone, working nonstop, never satisfied, asking who all the labor is even for. Then he says that if one trips, "the other can pull him to his feet." He also says how sad it is for "the one who trips with nobody to lift him!" This is wisdom from close to the ground. It is about work, falling, warmth, and danger, and about the mercy of not facing those things as a closed circle of one. The book can be stark about how much of life is a breath. Even so, it still honors the gift of a partner on the road. You were not made to prove that you can carry every bag without help.

So ask someone. If you have been carrying the bags alone, wait and walk with a neighbor, or accept the help you usually wave off. If you know a person who has been tripping in plain sight, be the one who pulls them to their feet this week. Two are better off than one, and you do not have to wait until a crisis to live as if that were true. A shared walk up the stairs, or a shared hour of work, can be the beginning of that kind of life.
entries.prayer: God, I have gotten too used to doing things alone. I carry the bags, I start the work, and I forget to ask. Thank you that two people are better off than one, and that you have not made me to be a closed circle. Show me who I should walk with, and who I should stop waving off. If someone near me is tripping, make me willing to pull them to their feet. If I am the one who has fallen, give me the humility to let a friend lift me. Bless the work we can do together, and keep me from the lonely pride that refuses help. Amen.

entries.title: On the Day I Am Afraid
entries.text:
On the day I am afraid,
I will lean on you.
entries.reflection:
Fear often arrives on a date you can already see coming. It shows up on the day of the appointment, in the parking lot, with your hands on the wheel and your mind already running ahead of the news you might hear. You may have slept badly. You may have arrived early just to sit in the car and feel the minutes pass, watching the clock and wishing you were already on the other side of the visit. The psalm does not ask you to wait until the fear has passed before you pray. "On the day I am afraid, I will lean on you."

David writes this while he is being trampled, not after the threat has gone. "Be kind to me, God, because people are trampling me." A verse later he says, "I trust God, so I have no fear. What could mere flesh do to me?" The courage is not a mood he has to manufacture first. He leans on the day he is afraid, and trust stands up inside that fear. Leaning is a physical picture. You put your weight on someone who can hold it. God is not waiting for you to become brave on your own and then come in. He is already able to bear the weight you are afraid to set down.

If you are in that parking lot today, or in any place where fear has arrived on schedule, lean now. Tell him what you are afraid to hear. Praise him for what he has promised, as this psalm does, even before the door opens. You may still feel the fear in your hands. You can lean anyway, and walk in as someone who is not facing mere flesh alone. When you come back to the car, lean again, whatever the news has been, and let him carry you home.
entries.prayer: God, this is a day I am afraid, and I will lean on you. You know the appointment, the parking lot, and the news I do not want to hear. Thank you that I do not have to wait until I feel brave to come to you. Be kind to me, as David asked, and hold the weight I cannot carry well. I trust you, and I ask for a steady heart before the door opens. Praise you for what you have promised. Walk with me from the car into the room, and do not let mere flesh be the largest thing in my sight. I lean on you now. Amen.

entries.title: A Friend at Every Moment
entries.text:
A friend loves at every moment.
A brother is born to help in hard times.
entries.reflection:
Friendship can shrink to convenient hours without anyone meaning it to. You mean to call, and then the week gets loud, and the name sits untouched on your phone. You pass it in the morning and again at night, and you tell yourself you will do better when you are less tired, though later keeps sliding away. The proverb is shorter than our excuses. "A friend loves at every moment. A brother is born to help in hard times."

This is a saying about loyalty, set among other observations about sense, speech, and the way people treat each other. Love at every moment does not mean you never sleep, or that you must fix every wound. It means friendship is not only for easy days, when conversation is light and no one needs much. A brother, in this line, is someone who shows up when the time is hard. Hard times are exactly when a person may start to believe they are too much trouble. The proverb answers that fear by saying a brother is born for that very kind of hour. You do not have to be impressive in the help you give. You have to be present.

Look at the names on your phone today and pick the one you have been postponing. If they are in a hard stretch, love them at this moment, not at a later moment that may never feel convenient. Send the message, or sit with them if you can. If you are the one in a hard time, you are allowed to let a friend in, instead of protecting them from your need. That is part of what a friend is for. A short, honest note can be a kind of arrival, and it can reach someone who thought no one would come.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, make me a friend who loves at every moment, not only when it is convenient. I have let names sit untouched on my phone, and I have told myself I would get to them later. Forgive my delay. Show me the person who is in a hard time, and give me the will to go toward them today. Thank you that you have given us brothers and friends for the hours that hurt. If I am the one who needs help, take away the pride that keeps people out. Teach me to receive love as well as give it. Let my friendship be loyal, and let it show up. Amen.

entries.title: When You Have Eaten Your Fill
entries.text: You will eat and be full, and you will praise Yahweh your God for the good land he gave you.
entries.reflection:
A full plate can make a person forgetful. You eat, you lean back, and the next thought is already about tomorrow's work or a holiday meal still to come. The room is warm, the dishes are waiting, and gratitude can slip away in the ease of having enough, almost before you notice it leaving. Moses speaks to a people about to enter a good land, and he tells them what to do with fullness. "You will eat and be full, and you will praise Yahweh your God for the good land he gave you."

The next word is a warning. "Take care not to forget Yahweh your God" He knows what happens "When you have eaten and are full, when you have built fine houses and settled in," Fullness is a gift, and it is also a test. Israel had been through hunger in the wilderness, and they were about to know plenty. The praise Moses asks for is more than decoration on a feast. This is how you remember the Giver when the land starts to feel like it was always yours. Yahweh gave the land. The food comes from his hand, even when your own work helped put it on the table. Plenty can feel so normal that you stop saying his name over it.

So tonight, when you have eaten and you are full, pause before the dishes. Praise him for the good land and for the meal, by name. If money has been tight, praise him for what is here anyway. If the table is already abundant, take care not to rush past him as if plenty were only normal. Forgetting is the easy road after a good supper. Remembering is an act of love, and it can start with a simple thank you before you stand up.
entries.prayer: Yahweh my God, I have eaten, and I want to praise you for the good land and for this meal. You know whether this table has felt abundant or tight, and you know how quickly I can forget you once I am full. Thank you that the food comes from your hand, even when my own work helped to put it here. Keep me from settling in as if the gift were only ordinary. I do not want to ignore your commands, or to treat plenty as if I had made it myself. Receive my thanks tonight, before I stand up and go on. Teach me to remember you in hunger and in fullness. Amen.

entries.title: Go In with Thanks
entries.text:
Go into his gates with thanks,
and into his courtyards with praise.
Thank him and bless his name.
entries.reflection:
You can walk into a crowded kitchen, or into a small room with only a few people, and already start comparing. The table looks different than you hoped. Someone is missing. A dish is late, or the conversation is thinner than last year's, and your mind begins to keep score before you have even sat down, already deciding the day has fallen short of what you wanted it to be. The psalm tells you how to go in anyway. "Go into his gates with thanks, and into his courtyards with praise. Thank him and bless his name."

This is a psalm for entering, a short call to worship that begins with gladness and with the reminder that Yahweh is God. "Serve Yahweh with joy. Come into his presence singing." The people are his flock, not a crowd that has to earn a place at the gate. And the reason for all this thanks is given in the last verse: "Yahweh is good. His faithful love lasts forever," and "his truth lasts through every generation." The courtyards belong to a good God. Thanks is how you walk toward him, even when the day in your house is less smooth than the song. You can bless his name before the gathering has proved itself to you.

If you enter a gathering today, enter with thanks on your mouth, not with a scorecard. Bless his name for the people who are there, and for his faithful love that has lasted into this year. If you are not walking into a large meal, you can still go into his presence with the same words. Thank him. Bless his name. The gates are not only for the impressive days. They are for this ordinary, uneven one as well, and his goodness has not run out.
entries.prayer: Yahweh, I want to go into your gates with thanks, and into your courtyards with praise. I bless your name. Some parts of this day look different than I hoped, and someone I love may be missing from the room. Still, you are good, and your faithful love lasts forever. Thank you that I do not have to earn a place in your presence. Thank you for the people who are here, and for your truth that lasts through every generation. Put thanks on my mouth as I walk in, and keep me from measuring the table against a picture I had in my head. I come to you with praise, and I ask you to meet us here. Amen.
